scenarios.name: Imaginative informational process with an unclear next step
scenarios.draft:
My Air Cleaner

My imagined machine cleans classroom air. A fan pulls air through a reusable filter. The filter catches dirt and tiny pieces of plastic. Then the clean air goes back into the room.
scenarios.assignment_prompt: Explain an imaginative machine that could help a classroom. No scientific source is required.
scenarios.teacher_directions: Explain the process clearly. Do not certify that the invention works.
scenarios.student_concerns: I want readers to follow my machine's steps.
scenarios.acceptance_focus: Anchor to an imaginative topic without inventing a factual claim, mechanism, or target answer
expected_outcomes: Use the proposed process as the focus and leave the missing process idea to the student.

strengths: The draft names the machine's purpose and an input-output sequence.

issues.description: The draft does not explain what the student proposes happens to the material caught by the filter.
issues.draft_reference: The filter catches dirt and tiny pieces of plastic.

revision_candidates.title: Clarify the next proposed step
revision_candidates.draft_reference: The filter catches dirt and tiny pieces of plastic.

scenarios.name: Short argument without a specific claim
scenarios.draft:
Gardens are good.

A garden would help our school.
scenarios.assignment_prompt: Argue whether our school should start a garden.
scenarios.teacher_directions: State a position and give a reason. Five paragraphs are not required.
scenarios.student_concerns: I am not sure my first sentence says what I think.
scenarios.acceptance_focus: Support focus development without writing the missing claim for the student
expected_outcomes: Refer to the topic or existing wording instead of inventing the student's position.

strengths: The draft introduces a clear topic.

issues.description: The opening praises gardens without stating what the student thinks the school should do.

scenarios.name: Narrative key moment with first-person references
scenarios.draft:
I waited with my friend before our performance.

My friend squeezed my hand and smiled at me. I felt better.
scenarios.assignment_prompt: Tell about a moment when someone helped you.
scenarios.teacher_directions: Use concrete actions and preserve your personal voice.
scenarios.acceptance_focus: Use a key moment rather than a claim and preserve first-person reference text exactly
expected_outcomes: Do not change my friend, my, or me inside the exact quotation.

strengths: The friend's action gives the reader a concrete sign of support.

issues.description: The emotional change is summarized without a concrete detail showing what felt different.
issues.draft_reference: My friend squeezed my hand and smiled at me. I felt better.

revision_candidates.title: Show what changed in the moment
revision_candidates.draft_reference: My friend squeezed my hand and smiled at me. I felt better.

scenarios.name: Obscuring sentence-boundary pattern
scenarios.draft:
The waves roared and my brother cried and Dad held him and I did not know what to do.

Then we built a sandcastle.
scenarios.teacher_directions: Language corrections are optional unless they obscure meaning.
scenarios.acceptance_focus: Teach one recognizable sentence-boundary pattern without rewriting the sentence
expected_outcomes: Use the exact combined-action reference and avoid a list of unrelated conventions fixes.

strengths: The draft presents a clear sequence of family events.

issues.description: The combined actions obscure where one action ends and the narrator's response begins.
issues.draft_reference: The waves roared and my brother cried and Dad held him and I did not know what to do.

revision_candidates.title: Clarify the sentence boundaries
revision_candidates.draft_reference: The waves roared and my brother cried and Dad held him and I did not know what to do.

scenarios.name: Informational revision with a supplied source
scenarios.draft:
Pollination helps plants reproduce.

Bees move pollen from one flower to another. The supplied passage explains that pollen reaches the stigma. This step matters because it allows fertilization to begin.
scenarios.assignment_prompt: Explain how pollination works using the supplied passage.
scenarios.teacher_directions: Use the source accurately and connect the process steps.
scenarios.source_material: Paragraph 2: Bees carry pollen between flowers. When pollen reaches a flower's stigma, fertilization can begin.
scenarios.student_concerns: I tried to connect the steps in this revision.
scenarios.acceptance_focus: Maintain a bounded source handoff and cross-field coherence on an informational revision
expected_outcomes: Acknowledge the observed connection and focus the remaining action on the student's next process link.

controlled_round.original_draft:
Pollination helps plants reproduce.

Bees move pollen from one flower to another. The supplied passage explains that pollen reaches the stigma.
strengths: The revision connects the stigma step to fertilization in bounded language.

issues.description: The explanation would be clearer if the student connected the bee's action to the arrival of pollen at the stigma in their own words.
issues.draft_reference: Bees move pollen from one flower to another. The supplied passage explains that pollen reaches the stigma.

revision_candidates.title: Connect the process steps
revision_candidates.draft_reference: Bees move pollen from one flower to another. The supplied passage explains that pollen reaches the stigma.

selected_goals.title: Connect the process steps
selected_goals.draft_reference: The supplied passage explains that pollen reaches the stigma.

selected_goal_observations.observation: The revision adds a bounded explanation of why the stigma step matters.
selected_goal_observations.evidence_reference: This step matters because it allows fertilization to begin.

goal_feedback.observation: You added an explanation of why the stigma step matters.

scenarios.name: Argument revision with unavailable source verification
scenarios.draft:
Our school should start later because students would be more alert.

The passage says students concentrate better. I added that this could help them participate in class discussions.
scenarios.assignment_prompt: Argue whether school should start later using the assigned passage.
scenarios.teacher_directions: Connect evidence to the claim and do not invent source content.
scenarios.student_concerns: I tried to explain the evidence.
scenarios.acceptance_focus: Preserve a missing-source limitation while giving student-authored revision guidance
expected_outcomes: Do not verify the passage or supply the missing source explanation.

controlled_round.original_draft:
Our school should start later because students would be more alert.

The passage says students concentrate better.
strengths: The revision adds the student's own possible classroom connection.

issues.description: The new discussion detail would help readers more if the student explained its connection to being alert in their own words.
issues.draft_reference: I added that this could help them participate in class discussions.

revision_candidates.title: Explain your classroom connection
revision_candidates.draft_reference: I added that this could help them participate in class discussions.

selected_goals.title: Explain your classroom connection
selected_goals.draft_reference: The passage says students concentrate better.

selected_goal_observations.observation: The revision adds a concrete classroom situation while leaving the causal connection open to further explanation.

goal_feedback.observation: You added a classroom situation and can now explain its connection in your own words.

source_limitations: The assigned passage was not supplied, so its content cannot be checked. Add the passage before verifying the reference.

scenarios.name: Source-based explanation requiring separated actions
scenarios.draft:
Our school should start a garden.

In the class survey, 62% of students said they would try garden vegetables. This supports our plan.
scenarios.assignment_prompt: Argue whether our school should start a garden using the supplied survey.
scenarios.teacher_directions: Explain what the survey shows and how it connects to the claim.
scenarios.source_material: A synthetic class survey of 50 students found that 31 would try vegetables from a school garden. The survey measured interest, not health outcomes.
scenarios.student_concerns: I need help explaining the number without repeating it.
scenarios.acceptance_focus: Split locating, interpreting, and connecting into manageable steps without supplying the interpretation
expected_outcomes: Keep the survey meaning and final warrant student-authored.

strengths: The draft includes a relevant survey result and a clear garden topic.

issues.description: The draft says the result supports the plan without explaining the student's interpretation or connection to the claim.
issues.draft_reference: In the class survey, 62% of students said they would try garden vegetables. This supports our plan.

revision_candidates.title: Explain the survey connection
revision_candidates.draft_reference: In the class survey, 62% of students said they would try garden vegetables. This supports our plan.

scenarios.name: Claim-less narrative key moment
scenarios.draft:
I stood outside the auditorium.

I opened the door and saw everyone looking at me. I walked to my seat.
scenarios.assignment_prompt: Tell about a time you felt nervous.
scenarios.teacher_directions: Develop one moment with actions or sensory details.
scenarios.acceptance_focus: Anchor feedback to a key moment without demanding a claim, citation, or counterclaim
expected_outcomes: Leave the imagined action or sensory detail to the student.

strengths: The draft establishes a clear place and sequence.

issues.description: The key entrance moment moves quickly without a concrete detail that shows the narrator's experience.
issues.draft_reference: I opened the door and saw everyone looking at me.

revision_candidates.title: Develop the entrance moment
revision_candidates.draft_reference: I opened the door and saw everyone looking at me.
